lines.text: Millions of us used them every day, and then one day they were gone. This is a timeline of discontinued tech, from the floppy disk to the apps of yesterday.
It begins in 1971 with the floppy disk. For three decades it carried our software and our homework, and it still lives on as the save icon.
In 1975 Sony brought out Betamax. Its picture was a little sharper, but its tapes held less, and in living rooms it lost the format war.
The winner arrived a year later. JVC's VHS became the tape of home video and Friday night rentals, until DVD finally pushed it aside.
Then came LaserDisc, a shining platter the size of a record with a crisp picture. It was the first optical disc on sale, but it never left its niche.
In 1979 Sony shrank the cassette player to fit a pocket. With the Walkman, music could go anywhere you did.
Meanwhile France went online years before the web. Minitel put a little terminal in homes for directories, banking and chat, and ran until 2012.
In 1981 IBM's new PC booted into MS-DOS. Microsoft had bought it from another firm, and for a decade it ran under almost every PC on Earth.
By 1984 your music had moved to shiny discs, and Sony's portable CD player let you carry them in a coat pocket, as long as you did not jog.
A year later Blockbuster opened its doors. At its peak thousands of stores rented tapes and DVDs, until mail rental and streaming emptied the shelves.
In 1991 Visual Basic let people drag and drop their way to a Windows program, and millions took their first steps in coding.
Sony tried again with MiniDisc, a tiny recordable disc in a plastic case. Japan loved it, but MP3 players overtook it.
In 1993 a whole encyclopedia fit on a CD. Microsoft's Encarta lasted until Wikipedia made it unnecessary.
Then the web opened up. Netscape Navigator brought it to the public and kicked off the dot com boom, and its code lives on in Firefox.
That same year GeoCities offered anyone a free home page. Millions built their first website there, with blinking pictures and visitor counters.
In 1995 Java applets promised rich apps inside a web page. They were slow to start and a constant security risk, and browsers turned them off.
The Iomega Zip disk held as much as seventy floppies. Every design studio had one, along with its dreaded click of death.
Microsoft answered Netscape with Internet Explorer, free with Windows. It won almost every user, then stalled, and was finally retired in 2022.
AltaVista was the first search engine that seemed to know the whole web. Then Google came along with better results, and it faded away.
In 1996 the PalmPilot put your contacts and calendar in your hand, and read your handwriting. It was the first handheld organiser most people wanted.
That year also brought Flash, the plug-in behind web games, cartoons and YouTube's first videos, until the iPhone refused it and HTML5 took its place.
Chat went worldwide with ICQ. Everyone had a number, and a little uh-oh sound told you a new message had arrived.
In North America, after school meant AIM: buddy lists, screen names and away messages crafted with great care.
And in Microsoft Office a paperclip popped up to offer help. Clippy was widely mocked, and quietly removed in 2007.
Yahoo had its own messenger too, with chat rooms, emoticons and a buzz that shook your friend's window.
On phones, Symbian powered Nokia's years at the top, until Android and the iPhone overtook it.
In 1998 Sega launched the Dreamcast, with a modem built in for online play. It was ahead of its time, but the PlayStation 2 ended Sega's console days.
A year later TiVo let you pause live television, record a whole series and skip the ads. For a while, to TiVo something was a verb.
Also in 1999, Napster launched from a college dorm. Millions swapped songs for free, until lawsuits shut it down and the music business changed for good.
Microsoft's messenger, with its nudges and winks, became how young people chatted across much of the world through the two thousands.
When Napster closed, LimeWire took up the swapping, and millions kept getting songs without paying.
So did Kazaa, until the music industry's lawsuits forced it to change, and then to close.
In 2001 Apple put a thousand songs in your pocket. The iPod changed how music was sold, until the iPhone swallowed it whole.
That same year came Windows XP, stable and long lived. People clung to it for more than a decade, past the end of its own support.
In 2003 Friendster became the first social network to reach millions. Its pages loaded slowly, and its users drifted to MySpace and Facebook.
Skype made calls across the world free, and its name came to mean a video call, until Zoom and phone apps took over.
Nokia tried a phone that was also a game console. The N-Gage was shaped like a taco, and dropped within two years.
In 2004 Google launched Orkut. Americans hardly noticed, but in Brazil and India it was the social network for years.
Megaupload stored and shared big files, many of them films and songs shared without permission, and became one of the busiest sites online.
On BlackBerry phones, BBM was free, fast and showed when your message had been read, years before other apps did.
Google Reader gathered every new post from the sites you followed. Its devoted fans still mourn it.
Children waddled into Club Penguin, decorating igloos and chatting with friends, and more than two hundred million accounts were made.
On Yahoo Answers anyone could ask and anyone could answer, giving real help, homework shortcuts and some gloriously strange questions.
In 2006 Toshiba's HD DVD fought Blu-ray for the future of film on disc, and lost in two years.
The Flip camera had one red button and a USB plug that flipped out. It made sharing video easy, just before phones did it better.
That same year Microsoft answered the iPod with the Zune. Five years late, it never came close.
In 2007 the BlackBerry Curve brought the little keyboard to everyone, and teenagers and office workers alike could not put it down.
Microsoft also launched Silverlight to take on Flash. Netflix streamed with it for a while, but browsers dropped plug-ins altogether.
In 2010 Kinect let Xbox players use their bodies and voices instead of a controller. It sold fast, and even found work in robotics labs.
Windows Phone arrived with bright tiles instead of icons, but it never won enough apps or users, and Microsoft gave up.
In 2011 Google took on Facebook with Google Plus. Plenty were signed up, but few stayed.
The Pebble watch was paid for by its fans on Kickstarter, a record at the time, and its e-paper screen ran for days on one charge.
Vine looped six second videos and invented a style of short comedy that TikTok would later make enormous.
Google Glass put a tiny screen over one eye. The backlash over privacy was swift.
In 2014 Microsoft gave Windows a voice assistant named after a Halo character. Cortana never caught up, and gave way to Copilot.
Windows 10 came as a free upgrade and ran on more than a billion devices. Many were still on it when its support ended in 2025.
Google Stadia streamed big games with no console at all. The technology worked, but too few people signed up.
And in 2020 Quibi raised almost two billion dollars for short phone videos, and closed just eight months later.
Every one of them was the future once. Somewhere, a drawer still holds a few.
